Malediction

mal-uh-DIK-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Malediction is a curse; a spoken wish for harm or misfortune to befall someone.

The dying pirate captain's malediction against the crew who had betrayed him was said to haunt the ship for decades.

Worked Example

Ancient court records describe a nobleman's malediction against the rival family he blamed for his son's death, sworn before witnesses in the city square.

A malediction isn't just an insult -- it's a formal, almost ritual curse meant to bring lasting harm.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

curse: a spoken wish for harm or misfortune

hex: a magic spell intended to cause harm

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

blessing: an expression of good wishes

benediction: a formal blessing, especially at the end of a ceremony

Where it sits · how severe the condemnation is — criticism → malediction → damnation

criticism vs. malediction: Criticism is a negative comment or judgment, much milder than a curse.

damnation vs. malediction: Damnation is condemnation to eternal punishment, an even more extreme curse.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — male-

prefix — male-: bad, badly (Latin)

root — diction

root — diction: the act of speaking (also a modern English word for manner of speaking or word choice) (Latin dicere, 'to say')

Put it together

Put it together: Malediction comes from Latin male- ('bad') + diction ('speaking') -- literally 'bad-speaking,' which came to mean a curse: words spoken to bring harm.

Use the root in a new word: diction

Use the root in a new word: diction: The radio announcer was admired for his crisp, clear diction.

Word Choice

Malediction is a formal, almost literary word for a curse -- you'll see it more often in fiction, folklore, or dramatic speech than in casual conversation.
